questions.title: Posterior mediastinum vagus nerve identification
questions.question: This arrow refers to…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The sympathetic trunk runs more laterally, on the rib necks/vertebral bodies, a different course from the vagus nerve pictured here.
explanations.B: Correct. The right and left vagus nerves take different paths through the mediastinum before breaking up behind their lung roots into the pulmonary and oesophageal plexuses. This is the structure this image identifies on a posterior-mediastinum cross-section. Distinguishing it from the neighbouring sympathetic trunk, phrenic nerve and thoracic duct is the skill this item tests.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The phrenic nerve runs anterior to the lung root (on the venous side on the right, arterial side on the left), a different position from the vagus nerve pictured here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The thoracic duct lies against the vertebral bodies, crossing to the left at T5, a deeper midline structure distinct from the vagus nerve.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the vagus nerve on a posterior-mediastinum cross-section, distinct from the sympathetic trunk, phrenic nerve and thoracic duct.

questions.title: Diaphragmatic esophageal opening contents (corrected from caval)
questions.question: This opening contains…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right phrenic nerve passes through the CAVAL opening (T8), a different, more lateral opening from the one pictured here.
explanations.B: Correct, and corrected from the Step-1 triage's initial "caval opening" label. The arrow sits on the smaller, more medial oesophageal opening (T10), which transmits the oesophagus and the anterior/posterior vagal trunks. This reading was confirmed by 200 dpi render against the visible aortic opening lower on the same plate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The azygos vein ascends through the aortic opening (T12) alongside the aorta and thoracic duct, not through the oesophageal opening.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The left phrenic nerve pierces the diaphragm on its own, separately from the three named openings, not through the oesophageal opening.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State that the vagi pass through the diaphragm's oesophageal opening, correcting an initial caval-opening misreading.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi; corrects the Step-1 triage's provisional caval-opening label, see coverage/AU-MED-106-anatomy-triage.md

questions.title: Internal thoracic artery termination
questions.question: This artery terminates at…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The 3rd costal cartilage is near the artery's course, not its termination point.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The 3rd intercostal space is far too high; the artery continues well past this level.
explanations.C: Correct. The internal thoracic artery descends behind the upper six costal cartilages to end opposite the SIXTH intercostal space. There it divides into the musculophrenic and superior epigastric arteries, its two terminal branches. Knowing this termination level is what lets a student place the artery correctly on a labelled thoracic-wall image.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The 6th costal cartilage is close to, but not exactly, the termination level; the artery ends opposite the 6th intercostal SPACE, not at the cartilage itself.

questions.learning_objective: State that the internal thoracic artery terminates opposite the sixth intercostal space, dividing into the musculophrenic and superior epigastric arteries.

questions.title: Bronchial tree at the root of the lung
questions.question: This arrow refers to…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The hyparterial bronchus (to the middle and lower lobes on the right) lies below and behind the pulmonary artery, a different position from the structure pointed to here.
explanations.B: Correct. At the root of the lung, the superior pulmonary vein lies most anteriorly, ahead of both the pulmonary artery and the principal bronchus. This is the arrangement this item's pointer identifies. The mnemonic order from front to back — vein, artery, bronchus — is the fact this item tests directly.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pulmonary artery lies in front of the bronchus but behind the pulmonary vein, a middle position rather than the most anterior one pictured here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The eparterial bronchus (to the right upper lobe) arises outside the hilum, above the pulmonary artery — a different structure from the one identified.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State the anteroposterior order of structures at the root of the lung: vein, artery, bronchus.

questions.title: Oblique fissure surface anatomy
questions.question: Surface anatomy of this structure

explanations.A: Incorrect. Starting from the 4th thoracic spine is close but not the printed surface marking; the accepted starting point is the 3rd spine.
explanations.B: Correct, as printed. The oblique fissure's surface marking runs from the spine of the 3rd thoracic vertebra to the 6th costal cartilage, present in both lungs. It separates the upper (and middle, on the right) lobe from the lower lobe. The left lung, having only this one fissure, has just two lobes against the right's three.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This range runs too low at both ends compared with the printed surface marking.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This range is too high and too short compared with the printed surface marking of the oblique fissure.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State the surface marking of the oblique fissure (3rd thoracic spine to 6th costal cartilage).

questions.title: Lingula identification
questions.question: This arrow refers to…lingula

options.C: Superior lobe of left lung, lingular part

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right lung's middle lobe is a separate lobe (between the oblique and horizontal fissures), the anatomical counterpart of the lingula but a distinct structure on the opposite lung.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cardiac notch is a deficiency in the anterior border of the left lung's superior lobe, adjacent to but not the same as the lingula itself.
explanations.C: Correct. The lingula is a tongue-shaped projection of the left lung's superior lobe, below the cardiac notch. It is the left lung's structural, though not lobar, counterpart to the right lung's middle lobe. Unlike the middle lobe, the lingula is not separated off by its own fissure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The oblique fissure is the boundary separating lobes, not a lobe or projection itself.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the lingula as a projection of the left lung's superior lobe, near the cardiac notch.

questions.title: Bronchial tree at the root of the lung (2nd instance)
questions.question: This arrow refers to…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The eparterial bronchus is specific to the RIGHT lung's superior lobe; this item's pointer identifies a different, more general structure.
explanations.B: Correct. This item identifies the left principal bronchus directly, rather than one of the right-sided eparterial/hyparterial subdivisions. This is consistent with the left bronchus having no eparterial branch of its own. Its superior lobar bronchus arises inside the lung, unlike the right's, which arises outside the hilum above the pulmonary artery.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pulmonary artery lies above and in front of the left bronchus, a different structure from the bronchus itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Hyparterial" is a term used for the right bronchial subdivisions below the eparterial branch; it does not apply the same way to the left principal bronchus, which the confirmed key selects instead.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the left principal bronchus at the root of the lung.

questions.title: Esophageal groove termination level (printed key kept as-is)
questions.question: Structure in this impression terminates at…

explanations.A: Incorrect. T8 is the level of the diaphragm's caval opening, not where the oesophageal groove's contents terminate on this reading.
explanations.B: Correct, as printed. The bank's own ink-marked key selects T12. Recorded exactly as keyed, though the anatomically expected level for the oesophagus reaching the diaphragm's oesophageal opening is T10, not T12; this discrepancy is recorded as printed per the lane's convention-clash rule rather than silently corrected.
explanations.C: Incorrect per the printed key, though anatomically this is the expected level for the oesophageal opening — see the note under option B.
explanations.D: Incorrect. L1 is well below the diaphragm, too low for any of the mediastinal impressions on the lung's surface.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Recognise the printed key for the oesophageal groove's termination level, and its discrepancy from the anatomically expected T10 level of the diaphragm's oesophageal opening.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi; printed key T12 not reconciled with the anatomically expected T10, per coverage/AU-MED-106-anatomy-triage.md's confirmed-key table

questions.title: Mediastinal surface impressions on the right lung (azygos arch)
questions.question: This impression contains…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right ventricle forms part of the cardiac impression on the mediastinal surface, a different, more anterior impression from the one this item points to.
explanations.B: Correct. The mediastinal surface of the right lung is grooved by the arch of the azygos vein, which arches over the root of the lung before draining into the SVC. This is one of the named impressions distinguishing the right lung's mediastinal surface from the left's. The left lung's mediastinal surface is grooved instead by the aortic arch and its two great branches.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The IVC grooves the right lung's mediastinal surface at a separate, lower impression from the azygos arch pictured here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The right phrenic nerve runs in its own groove near the SVC/IVC impressions, distinct from the azygos arch impression this item identifies.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the azygos arch impression on the right lung's mediastinal surface.

questions.title: Mediastinal surface impressions on the right lung (phrenic nerve)
questions.question: …structure passes through this structure (second point on the same p.13 image)

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right vagus nerve runs a separate course through the superior mediastinum before breaking up behind the lung root, a different structure from the one pointed to here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The LEFT phrenic nerve grooves the LEFT lung's mediastinal surface (arterial side of the mediastinum), not the right lung's impression pictured here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sympathetic trunk runs along the posterior mediastinum, not through this particular mediastinal-surface impression on the lung.
explanations.D: Correct. The right phrenic nerve runs on the venous side of the mediastinum, grooving the right lung's mediastinal surface near the SVC/IVC impressions. It then pierces the diaphragm's caval opening, its own point of entry into the abdomen. The left phrenic nerve, by contrast, runs on the arterial side of the mediastinum and grooves the left lung's mediastinal surface instead.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the right phrenic nerve's impression on the right lung's mediastinal surface.

questions.title: Intercostal muscle layer identification
questions.question: This arrow refers to…

options.D: Innermost intercostal muscle (2nd option, illegible distractor recorded as printed)

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Sternocostal muscle" is not one of the three standard intercostal layers; transversus thoracis (sternocostalis) lies on the inner chest wall near the sternum, a different muscle from the one pictured here.
explanations.B: Correct. The external intercostal muscle is the outermost of the three intercostal layers, running obliquely between the ribs. It is the layer this item's pointer identifies, and it acts as the main inspiratory elevator of the rib. This action distinguishes it functionally from the deeper internal and innermost layers.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The innermost intercostal muscle is the deepest of the three layers, separated from the external layer (pictured here) by the internal intercostal muscle and the neurovascular bundle.
explanations.D: Incorrect (illegible distractor, recorded as printed per the triage — the fourth option's text could not be fully read even at 200 dpi).

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the external intercostal muscle as the outermost, main inspiratory layer.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi; option C's illegible duplicate recorded as printed, see coverage/AU-MED-106-anatomy-triage.md

questions.title: Pericardial sinus identification
questions.question: Options: oblique sinus / separation Pulm. trunk–aorta / separation SVC–atrium / separation SVC–aorta

options.B: Separation between the SVC and right atrium
options.C: Separation between the SVC and left atrium
options.D: Transverse sinus, separating the arterial (aorta/pulmonary trunk) and venous (SVC) ends of the heart

explanations.A: Incorrect. The oblique sinus is a DIFFERENT pericardial recess, a blind pouch behind the left atrium, not the separation this item's confirmed key describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The SVC drains directly into the right atrium with no pericardial sinus separating them at this point.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The SVC does not drain into the left atrium at all, so no such separation exists.
explanations.D: Correct, as confirmed at 200 dpi render. The transverse sinus of the pericardium passes between the arterial end of the heart (aorta and pulmonary trunk) and the venous end (SVC). Surgeons use this passage to control the great vessels during cardiac surgery. It is distinct from the oblique sinus, a blind pouch behind the left atrium.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the transverse sinus of the pericardium as the passage between the heart's arterial and venous ends.

questions.title: Coronary vessel termination/anastomosis
questions.question: This vessel terminates…

options.A: Anastomoses with the anterior interventricular artery
options.C: Anastomoses with the left coronary artery directly
options.D: Anastomosis with continuation of right coronary artery

explanations.A: Incorrect. Anastomosis with the anterior interventricular artery describes a different coronary territory boundary, not the one this item's confirmed key describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Ends in the coronary sinus" describes a cardiac VEIN's termination, not an artery's anastomosis, which is what this item is asking about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Coronary arteries anastomose functionally at capillary level but this option misdescribes the specific relationship the confirmed key names.
explanations.D: Correct, as confirmed. This vessel (in the coronary sulcus, on the posterior/inferior aspect of the heart) anastomoses with the continuation of the right coronary artery. Consistent with the right coronary artery's course around the coronary sulcus to give the posterior interventricular artery, completing the coronary circulation's posterior territory.

questions.learning_objective: State that the circumflex/left coronary territory anastomoses with the right coronary artery's continuation around the coronary sulcus.

questions.title: Tracheal bifurcation level (recovered)
questions.question: This arrow refers to the level of… (recovered at 200 dpi, previously unreadable)

explanations.A: Incorrect. T2 is too high; it is roughly the level of the manubriosternal joint's superior aspect, above the bifurcation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. T6 is too low for the tracheal bifurcation.
explanations.C: Correct. The trachea bifurcates at the sternal angle into right and left principal bronchi, approximately the T4/T5 vertebral level. This is the level this recovered item's confirmed key identifies. The sternal angle is therefore a useful surface landmark for both the tracheal bifurcation and several nearby mediastinal structures.
explanations.D: Incorrect. T8 is the level of the diaphragm's caval opening, well below the tracheal bifurcation.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State that the trachea bifurcates at the sternal angle, approximately T4.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi (page recovered; Step-1 triage had flagged it text-extraction-unreadable)

questions.title: Right atrium venous opening identification (recovered)
questions.question: This arrow refers to… (recovered at 200 dpi, previously unreadable)

explanations.A: Incorrect. The coronary sinus opens into the right atrium at a separate, more inferomedial point, guarded by the valve of the coronary sinus, not the opening this item's confirmed key identifies.
explanations.B: Correct. The right atrium's venous openings include the SVC (superiorly), the IVC (inferiorly, guarded by the valve of the IVC/Eustachian valve) and the coronary sinus. This recovered item identifies the IVC opening specifically.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The fossa ovalis is a depression on the atrial septum, not a venous opening, and is confirmed on the neighbouring recovered item (p.22) instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The crista terminalis is the ridge separating the atrium proper from the sinus venarum, not a venous opening itself.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the IVC's opening into the right atrium.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi (page recovered; Step-1 triage had flagged it text-extraction-unreadable)

questions.title: Fossa ovalis identification (recovered)
questions.question: This arrow refers to… (recovered at 200 dpi, previously unreadable)

explanations.A: Correct. The fossa ovalis, a shallow depression on the interatrial septum bounded by the limbus fossae ovalis, is the postnatal remnant of the fetal foramen ovale. This is the structure this recovered item's confirmed key identifies. Its position on the septal (not lateral) wall distinguishes it from the crista terminalis and pectinate muscles nearby.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The crista terminalis is a ridge on the lateral (not septal) wall of the right atrium, separating the rough atrium proper from the smooth sinus venarum.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pectinate muscles are the comb-like ridges of the rough atrium proper, on the anterior/lateral wall, not the septal depression pictured here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The sinus venarum is the smooth-walled part of the right atrium receiving the great veins, a region rather than the specific septal landmark this item identifies.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the fossa ovalis on the interatrial septum as the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi (page recovered; Step-1 triage had flagged it text-extraction-unreadable)

questions.title: Azygos arch tributary level (recovered)
questions.question: This structure ends at the level of… (recovered at 200 dpi, azygos arch tributary)

explanations.A: Correct. The azygos arch curves over the root of the right lung to end at the level of the sternal angle (manubriosternal joint), draining into the SVC. The level this recovered item's confirmed key identifies, and one this bank's own posterior-intercostal/azygos-hemiazygos items (see the sparse-updated Kasr concept CON-CVS-19E63D8A8E7EDA) also test from a related angle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The xiphisternal joint is well below the azygos arch's termination, at the lower end of the sternum.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The jugular notch is at the top of the manubrium, above the sternal angle, too high for the azygos arch's termination level.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The T4/T5 disc level is the same general plane as the sternal angle but describes a posterior vertebral landmark, not the specific level the confirmed key names for this anterior venous structure.

questions.subtopic: Great Veins of the Neck and Thorax
questions.learning_objective: State that the azygos arch ends at the sternal angle level, draining into the SVC.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi (page recovered; Step-1 triage had flagged it text-extraction-unreadable)

questions.title: Right-sided venous valve, embryological origin (recovered/duplicated on p.26)
questions.question: This structure is the embryological remnant of… (recovered at 200 dpi; duplicated with the same stem/options/mark on page 26)

options.A: Left horn of the sinus venosus
options.D: Right valve of the sinuatrial orifice

explanations.A: Incorrect. The left horn of the sinus venosus becomes the coronary sinus, a different structure from the right-sided venous valve this item's confirmed key identifies.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The bulbus cordis contributes to the right ventricle's proximal part and the roots of the great vessels, not the atrial valve pictured here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Septum primum contributes to the atrial septum and the flap valve of the foramen ovale, a different embryological derivative from the structure identified.
explanations.D: Correct, as confirmed at 200 dpi. This structure is the embryological derivative of the right valve of the sinuatrial orifice, part of the sinus venosus's original paired valves. This is consistent with the right atrium's smooth-walled sinus venarum deriving from the absorbed right horn of the sinus venosus. The same item appears identically on page 26, a genuine duplicate rather than a second distinct question.

questions.learning_objective: State the embryological origin of a right-atrial venous valve remnant from the right valve of the sinuatrial orifice.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi (page recovered; duplicated identically on page 26, authored once here)

questions.title: Right ventricle internal feature identification
questions.question: This structure is called…

explanations.A: Incorrect. Papillary muscles are conical projections anchoring the chordae tendineae, a different structure from the muscular band this item identifies.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Trabeculae carneae are the irregular muscular ridges lining the right ventricle's inflow part generally, not the single, distinctive band this item points to.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chordae tendineae are thin fibrous cords connecting papillary muscles to the valve cusps, structurally unlike the thick muscular band this item identifies.
explanations.D: Correct. The moderator band is a distinctive muscular bridge crossing the right ventricular cavity, carrying part of the right bundle branch of the conducting system to the anterior papillary muscle. It is a specific, recognisable structure among the right ventricle's internal features. Its role in conducting the impulse to the anterior papillary muscle is what makes it clinically as well as anatomically notable.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the moderator band among the right ventricle's internal features.

questions.title: Azygos/hemiazygos system tributary identification
questions.question: This arrow refers to…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right superior intercostal vein drains directly into the azygos vein, on the opposite side from the vessel this item points to.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The suprascapular vein drains the scapular region into the subclavian vein, unrelated to the azygos/hemiazygos posterior intercostal system pictured here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Individual left posterior intercostal veins (below the first two or three) drain into the hemiazygos system, but this specific labelled vessel is the collecting superior intercostal vein, not a single numbered posterior intercostal vein.
explanations.D: Correct. The posterior intercostal veins end differently on the two sides: on the right, directly into the azygos system; on the left, the upper ones collect into the left superior intercostal vein, which drains into the left brachiocephalic vein rather than directly into the azygos vein. This is the asymmetry this item's pointer identifies. The same asymmetry is the fact recorded on the sparse-updated Kasr concept CON-CVS-19E63D8A8E7EDA.

questions.subtopic: Great Veins of the Neck and Thorax
questions.learning_objective: State that the left superior intercostal vein collects the upper left posterior intercostal veins and drains into the left brachiocephalic vein, unlike the right side's direct azygos drainage.

questions.title: Cardiac plexus identification near the arch of aorta
questions.question: Which… structure is found on the right side of the pointed structure

explanations.A: Incorrect. The deep cardiac plexus lies more posteriorly, between the arch of the aorta and the tracheal bifurcation, a different plexus from the one this item's confirmed key identifies.
explanations.B: Correct. The superficial cardiac plexus lies below the arch of the aorta, in front of the ligamentum arteriosum or the right pulmonary artery — the plexus this item's confirmed key places to the right of the pointed structure. The heart's autonomic supply is parasympathetic from the two vagi and sympathetic from the upper five thoracic segments, meeting in these superficial and deep plexuses that only modulate heart rate, never initiate it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the right subclavian artery, not the arch of the aorta (that is the LEFT recurrent laryngeal nerve's relation), so it is not positioned here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Vagus nerve" is too generic for this specific plexus-identification item, which the confirmed key resolves to the superficial cardiac plexus by name.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the superficial cardiac plexus near the arch of the aorta.

questions.title: Aortic vestibule identification
questions.question: This arrow refers to…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The mitral valve's cusps guard the left atrioventricular orifice, at the INFLOW part of the left ventricle, not the smooth-walled outflow region pictured here.
explanations.B: Correct. The aortic vestibule is the smooth-walled, fibrous part of the left ventricle's outflow tract, immediately below the aortic valve. It is distinct from the left ventricle's inflow part, with its two papillary muscles feeding the mitral valve, and from the right ventricle's own outflow, the pulmonary infundibulum. Keeping these three regions separate is the point this item tests.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pulmonary infundibulum is the RIGHT ventricle's smooth-walled outflow part, leading to the pulmonary valve, not the left-ventricular structure this item points to.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The tricuspid valve's cusps guard the right atrioventricular orifice, an entirely different chamber from the one pictured here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the aortic vestibule as the left ventricle's smooth-walled outflow tract, distinct from the mitral valve cusps and the pulmonary infundibulum.

questions.title: Diaphragmatic caval opening level (recovered)
questions.question: Diaphragmatic opening level (recovered at 200 dpi, previously unreadable)

explanations.A: Incorrect. T10 is the level of the oesophageal opening, not the caval opening this recovered item's confirmed key identifies.
explanations.B: Correct. The diaphragm's caval opening, transmitting the IVC and the right phrenic nerve, is the highest and most anterior of the three major openings, at the level of T8. This level sits between the oesophageal opening (T10) and the aortic opening (T12), the diaphragm's other two named openings. Remembering the mnemonic "I ate ten eggs at twelve" (IVC-T8, oesophagus-T10, aorta-T12) keeps the three levels in order.
explanations.C: Incorrect. T12 is the level of the aortic opening, the lowest and most posterior of the three, not the caval opening pictured here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. T6 is above the diaphragm entirely, too high for any of its three named openings.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State that the diaphragm's caval opening, transmitting the IVC and right phrenic nerve, is at T8.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi (page recovered; Step-1 triage had flagged it text-extraction-unreadable)

questions.title: Thoracic duct cervical termination (recovered)
questions.question: This structure terminates at… (recovered at 200 dpi, previously unreadable)

explanations.A: Correct. The thoracic duct crosses from right to left behind the oesophagus at T5, then ascends into the neck to terminate at the level of C7. It drains into the left brachiocephalic vein, typically at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins. This termination is why a left-sided neck injury near this junction risks a chyle leak.
explanations.B: Incorrect. T1 is below the duct's actual cervical termination level.
explanations.C: Incorrect. C5 is too high in the neck for the duct's termination.
explanations.D: Incorrect. T4 is the level in the thorax where the duct is still crossing behind the oesophagus, not its final cervical termination point.

questions.subject: haem
questions.subtopic: Great Veins of the Neck and Thorax
questions.learning_objective: State that the thoracic duct terminates at C7 into the left brachiocephalic vein.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi (page recovered; Step-1 triage had flagged it text-extraction-unreadable)

questions.title: Diaphragmatic aortic opening level (recovered)
questions.question: Aortic opening level (recovered at 200 dpi, previously unreadable)

explanations.A: Incorrect. T10 is the level of the oesophageal opening, not the aortic opening this recovered item's confirmed key identifies.
explanations.B: Correct. The diaphragm's aortic opening, transmitting the aorta, the azygos vein and the thoracic duct, is the lowest and most posterior of the three major openings, at the level of T12. It lies behind rather than through the muscular diaphragm, which is why the aorta is never compressed by diaphragmatic contraction. This distinguishes it from the oesophageal opening, which does pass through muscle and can be the site of a hiatus hernia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. T8 is the level of the caval opening, the highest of the three, not the aortic opening pictured here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. L1 is below the diaphragm entirely, too low for the aortic opening.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State that the diaphragm's aortic opening, transmitting the aorta, azygos vein and thoracic duct, is at T12.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi (page recovered; Step-1 triage had flagged it text-extraction-unreadable)

questions.title: Arch of aorta relation identification (recovered)
questions.question: This arrow refers to… (recovered at 200 dpi, previously unreadable)

explanations.A: Correct. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve leaves the vagus on the aortic arch and hooks beneath it, beside the ligamentum arteriosum, before ascending in the tracheo-oesophageal groove. This is the nerve this recovered item's confirmed key identifies at the arch of the aorta. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve, by contrast, hooks under the right subclavian artery instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the right SUBCLAVIAN artery, not the arch of the aorta, so it would not be pictured at this location.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The left phrenic nerve passes anterior to the lung root, not hooking under the arch of the aorta like the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The vagus nerve trunk continues past this point; the specific branch hooking under the arch is the recurrent laryngeal nerve, not the parent trunk.

questions.learning_objective: State that the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks beneath the arch of the aorta beside the ligamentum arteriosum.

questions.title: Diaphragmatic crus identification (recovered, largely illegible)
questions.question: Right crus (recovered at 200 dpi; mostly illegible aside from a "Caudal" orientation label)

explanations.A: Correct, as confirmed at 200 dpi despite the stem's otherwise poor legibility. The right crus of the diaphragm is longer than the left, arising from the bodies of L1-L3 (versus L1-L2 for the left). Its fibres, along with the left crus's, decussate around the oesophageal opening, contributing to the physiological sphincter that helps prevent reflux.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The left crus is shorter, arising only from L1-L2, and is not the structure this recovered item's confirmed key identifies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The costal origin is a separate part of the diaphragm's attachment (from the lower six ribs/costal cartilages), not the vertebral crus pictured here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The central tendon is the trifoliate aponeurotic centre the muscular fibres converge on, not one of the crura themselves.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the right crus of the diaphragm.

questions.title: Coronary artery course identification
questions.question: This structure is accompanied by…in its course

explanations.A: Incorrect. The posterior interventricular artery runs in the posterior interventricular groove, a different course from the vessel this item's confirmed key identifies as its companion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Left coronary artery" names the PARENT vessel, not the specific companion branch accompanying the structure in this item's coronary sulcus course.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The left marginal artery runs along the heart's obtuse margin, related to but not the same course as the vessel identified here.
explanations.D: Correct. The circumflex artery, a branch of the left coronary artery, runs in the coronary sulcus, accompanying the great cardiac vein and other structures in that groove. It courses toward the posterior aspect of the heart, supplying the left atrium and part of the left ventricle. This companion course in the coronary sulcus is what page 44's second labelled point (ink-q44b) tests, identifying the right coronary artery running the same groove on the opposite side.

questions.learning_objective: State that the circumflex artery runs in the coronary sulcus as a branch of the left coronary artery.

questions.title: Coronary artery branch identification
questions.question: This arrow refers to… (second point on the same p.44 image)

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right marginal artery is a BRANCH of the right coronary artery, along the heart's acute margin, a smaller and more specific vessel than the one this item's confirmed key identifies.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The left coronary artery divides into the anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries, a different vessel from the one this second point on the p.44 image identifies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The circumflex artery is confirmed as the answer to the first point on this same image (ink-q44); this second point's confirmed key identifies a different vessel.
explanations.D: Correct. The right coronary artery runs the coronary sulcus to give the marginal and posterior interventricular arteries, supplying the whole right side of the heart and, in most people, the whole conducting system. This is the vessel this second labelled point on the p.44 image identifies. The neighbouring first point on the same image (ink-q44) instead identifies the circumflex artery.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the right coronary artery in the coronary sulcus, distinct from the circumflex artery labelled on the same image.

questions.title: Coronary sinus tributary identification
questions.question: What is the tributary of this vein

explanations.A: Incorrect. The internal jugular vein is a neck vein unrelated to the coronary sinus's cardiac tributaries.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The anterior cardiac veins drain DIRECTLY into the right atrium, bypassing the coronary sinus entirely — a common distractor precisely because it sounds like it should be a coronary sinus tributary but is not.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The venae cordis minimi (smallest cardiac veins) drain directly into the cardiac chambers, not into the coronary sinus.
explanations.D: Correct. Most cardiac veins end in the coronary sinus, which lies in the posterior coronary sulcus and receives the great, middle and small cardiac veins and the oblique vein of the left atrium. This is the tributary this item's confirmed key identifies. The anterior cardiac veins, by contrast, bypass the coronary sinus and drain directly into the right atrium.

questions.learning_objective: Name the oblique vein of the left atrium as a coronary sinus tributary, distinct from the anterior cardiac veins which bypass it.

questions.title: Right atrium internal feature identification
questions.question: Options only: papillary muscle / pectinate muscle / cristae terminalis / trabeculae carneae

options.A: Fossa ovalis (illegible 5th distractor recorded as printed)

explanations.A: Incorrect. The fossa ovalis is a septal depression, structurally unlike the ridged muscular pattern this item's confirmed key identifies.
explanations.B: Correct. The pectinate muscles are the comb-like muscular ridges lining the rough atrium proper (anterior/lateral wall) of the right atrium, anterior to the crista terminalis. This is the structure this item identifies, distinguishing the rough atrium proper from the smooth-walled sinus venarum behind it. The crista terminalis itself marks the boundary between these two regions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The crista terminalis is the single ridge SEPARATING the pectinate-muscle-lined atrium proper from the smooth sinus venarum, not the repeating ridged pattern itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Trabeculae carneae are the equivalent ridged pattern in the VENTRICLES, not the right atrium's own pectinate muscles pictured here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify pectinate muscles as the right atrium's own ridged pattern, distinct from ventricular trabeculae carneae.

questions.title: Arch of aorta relation identification (2nd instance, recovered)
questions.question: This arrow refers to… (recovered at 200 dpi, second image of the same idea as p.40)

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the right subclavian artery, not the arch of the aorta pictured on this second confirming image.
explanations.B: Correct, confirming the same relation as p.40 on a second image. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve leaves the vagus on the aortic arch and hooks beneath it beside the ligamentum arteriosum before ascending in the tracheo-oesophageal groove. This second confirming image reinforces the same course rather than testing a new fact.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The left phrenic nerve runs anterior to the lung root rather than hooking under the arch, a different course from the nerve pictured here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The vagus nerve trunk continues past this point; the specific branch hooking under the arch is the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.title: Right ventricle internal feature identification (2nd instance)
questions.question: This arrow refers to…

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pectinate muscles are the right ATRIUM's own ridged pattern, not the ventricular structure pictured here.
explanations.B: Correct. Trabeculae carneae are the irregular muscular ridges lining the right ventricle's inflow part. This is the structure this item's confirmed key identifies, distinguishing the right ventricle's rough inflow region from its smooth infundibulum (outflow part). The same contrast between rough inflow and smooth outflow also applies to the left ventricle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Papillary muscles are the conical projections anchoring the chordae tendineae to the valve cusps, a more specific and distinct structure from the general ridged trabeculae carneae pattern pictured here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chordae tendineae are the thin fibrous cords connecting papillary muscles to valve cusps, structurally unlike the muscular ridges this item identifies.

questions.learning_objective: Identify trabeculae carneae as the right ventricle's ridged inflow-part lining.

questions.title: Coronary sinus tributary identification (2nd instance)
questions.question: …structure passes through this structure

explanations.A: Incorrect. The middle cardiac vein runs in the posterior interventricular groove to reach the coronary sinus, a different, more posterior tributary from the one this item's confirmed key identifies.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The anterior cardiac veins drain directly into the right atrium, bypassing the coronary sinus entirely.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The small cardiac vein runs in the coronary sulcus alongside the right coronary artery, a separate tributary from the one identified here.
explanations.D: Correct. The great cardiac vein runs in the anterior interventricular groove alongside the anterior interventricular artery, then continues in the coronary sulcus to become the coronary sinus's main tributary. This is the vessel this item's confirmed key identifies. Its course alongside the anterior interventricular artery mirrors the artery's own supply territory.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the great cardiac vein as the main coronary sinus tributary running with the anterior interventricular artery.
